To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
corticosterone contributes to the consolidation of long-term contextual-fearing conditioning, and that this effect is specific to the context, not the cue.

(1) Adrenalectomy impairs long-term contextual-fearing conditioning, (2) this deficit is due to the loss of corticosterone, (3) corticosterone replacement after the conditioning episode can rescue this deficit, and (4) the effects of corticosterone on fear conditioning are selective, as corticosterone replacement does not affect immediate auditory-cue fear-conditioning or long-term contextual-far conditioning in rats exposed to the conditioning context prior to adrenalectomy

corticosterone is not necessary for immediate contextual- or auditory-cue fear learning, but is required for the consolidation of a memory representation of the contextual cues that supports long-term contextual-fearing.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the neurobiology of memory.
the neurobiological processes that underlie learning and memory.
the role of stress hormones, especially corticosterone, in the formation and consolidation of long-term memory.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the role of corticosterone in fear conditioning is to facilitate the long-term consolidation of a contextual memory representation.
corticosterone is not necessary for the formation of a contextual-fear memory but is essential for its consolidation.
corticosterone's contribution to fear conditioning is selective.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
corticosterone is not essential for the formation of a memory representation of the conditioning context.
corticosterone is not necessary for the acquisition of contextual fear conditioning.
corticosterone plays a role in the formation of a long-term contextual representation of fear.
The main takeaway from our work is that
stress hormones can have very different roles depending on the timing of the stressor relative to the memory task and the nature of the memory being formed.
the stress hormone, corticosterone, is not necessary for the initial formation of fear conditioning.
corticosterone is necessary for the consolidation of a contextual fear memory.
